claims.text: A multi-fidelity machine-learning model trained on defect-inclusive ab initio simulations and experimental conductivity data will predict bulk HfNbTaTiZr conductivity more accurately than traditional analytical models.
The proposed model is applicable to both nominally clean HfNbTaTiZr and HfNbTaTiZr containing approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
The model will combine ab initio simulations containing defect states with experimental conductivity measurements.
Oxygen content, defect density, microstructural inhomogeneity, and temperature-dependent scattering mechanisms will be explicit model inputs.
Impurity and quantum scattering dominate electrical transport in HfNbTaTiZr over 0–200 K.
Phonon scattering and defect mobility are significant in HfNbTaTiZr over 300–1200 K.
Impurity levels and defect scattering centers mediate electron transport and modify conductivity relative to a perfect-crystal prediction.
Approximately 1 wt.% oxygen alters electron pathways and carrier mobility through additional scattering.
Learning temperature-dependent defect effects from simulations and measurements will allow the model to capture scattering omitted by conventional analytical models.
The model will predict conductivity within approximately 10% of measured values in both specified temperature regimes.
Oxygen impurity scattering reduces low-temperature conductivity.
High-temperature conductivity reflects temperature-activated phonon and defect scattering.
Existing analytical conductivity predictions generally assume perfect, defect-free crystals.
Existing analytical predictions typically deviate significantly from measurements on samples with realistic defect contents.
The model is expected to be robust within 0–200 K and 300–1200 K.
Accuracy above 1200 K may be limited by unmodeled extreme defect mobility.
Extrapolation beyond the training-data domain and incomplete representation of microstructure may reduce model accuracy.
Held-out conductivity measurements on near-ideal and approximately 1 wt.% oxygen specimens across both temperature regimes will serve as the benchmark.
The hypothesis is falsified if predictions for the approximately 1 wt.% oxygen specimen differ from measurements by more than about 10% in either temperature regime.
The hypothesis is also falsified if the model fails to reproduce the differing conductivity trends of near-ideal and oxygenated specimens.
